title: Reading a proton-flux chart
purpose: Teach what the 2017 GOES curve measures, how to read a log scale and why shelter must be ready before the alarm.

beats.label: measured
beats.credit: NOAA GOES-13 hourly means · flare time NASA DONKI

beats.label: measured
beats.moon: The Moon: no air, no magnetic shield
beats.note: A count of protons, not a dose

captions: A weather satellite near Earth counts tiny, fast bits of the Sun: protons.
Its count is in pfu: protons per square centimetre, each second.
On a normal scale, a quiet day is so small you cannot even see it.
On a log scale, each step up is ten times bigger. Now both fit!
{flare_day}: an {flare_class} flare bursts on the Sun at {flare_start}.
At {storm_cross}, the protons cross the storm line: 10 pfu.
That is just {lead_words} minutes after the flare began.
Then they stay high for days, peaking at {peak} pfu!
The Moon has no air or magnetic shield, so storms like this reach the ground.
ends_on: When the alarm sounds, the protons are already on their way. Get the shelter ready before it!
